planting.note: Plant in evenly moist, sharply drained soil and avoid letting the root zone dry out during the growing season.

directions: This Caucasus-native alpine gentian forms a low, spreading cushion of glossy emerald foliage studded with upward-facing cobalt-blue trumpets with bright white throats from midsummer into fall. It is more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many alpine gentians, making it workable in rock gardens and border edges well beyond typical mountain-garden climates. Grow in full sun to light shade in evenly moist, sharply drained soil, and avoid letting it dry out during the growing season. Its compact habit suits troughs, scree beds, and the front of a perennial border.

common_name: Narrow-Leafed Snow Tussock (Rare New Zealand Grass)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and be patient, since this tussock is slow to establish but very long-lived once settled.

directions: Narrow-leafed snow tussock is an uncommon New Zealand native grass that builds dense, tawny-green tufts of fine arching blades, topped in summer by wiry stems carrying silvery seed panicles that persist into winter. It is slow to establish but very long-lived once settled, and tolerates more cold than its alpine origin might suggest. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, either as a textural specimen or massed for a meadow effect. Minimal care is needed beyond an occasional tidy of old foliage in late winter.

planting.note: Give it a sheltered, sunny spot with sharp drainage since its large size needs room and wind protection to keep good winter form.

directions: Mauritania vine reed is a massive Mediterranean bunchgrass forming an evergreen mound of tough, fine-textured blades traditionally twisted into rope and basketry. From summer into fall it sends up tall arching stems topped with pearly, purple-flushed plumes that sway above the foliage and draw seed-eating birds. It needs full sun, sharp drainage, and a sheltered spot to look its best through winter, since its size makes it a bold focal point rather than a background plant. Once established it is very drought tolerant and essentially maintenance-free.

planting.note: Site in bright shade with sheltered, acidic, well-drained soil; it dislikes both strong sun and waterlogged roots.

directions: This evergreen Ericaceae hybrid, raised from Himalayan foothill species, develops a woody base with swollen tubers and arching stems of glossy, huckleberry-like leaves flushed red when new. In summer it hangs clusters of creamy white, lantern-shaped flowers patterned with a fine maroon checkerboard, best appreciated at eye level. Grow in bright shade with sheltered, acidic, well-drained soil, as it resents both strong sun and waterlogging. Its arching form suits a large hanging container or a sheltered woodland-edge planting among ferns.

planting.note: Plant in full sun on lean, dry soil; it tolerates coastal wind and salt but may need winter protection at the cold edge of its range.

directions: Shrubby hare's ear is a tough Mediterranean evergreen shrub that builds a dense, rounded mound of leathery, sea-green leaves with gray undersides, distinct from the smaller annual Bupleurum species already in gardens. From midsummer into fall it carries airy clusters of small sulfur-yellow flowers that attract pollinators and add a soft haze of color above the foliage. It thrives in full sun on poor, dry soils and shrugs off coastal wind and salt spray, making it a reliable screen or windbreak where little else succeeds. Established plants need almost no supplemental water and little pruning beyond occasional shaping.

planting.note: Train against a sheltered, south- or west-facing wall in full sun to partial shade, since it dislikes both intense heat and hard freezes.

directions: This variegated sport of the Chilean boxleaf azara carries small, glossy leaves edged in creamy white along gracefully arching branches, giving a refined, airy texture year-round beyond the plain-green straight species. In early spring it produces small vanilla-scented flowers tucked along the stems, a pleasant surprise before most shrubs wake up. It grows slowly and prefers a sheltered, warm wall with full sun to partial shade, since it dislikes both intense heat and hard freezes. Train it against a south- or west-facing wall for best winter protection and prune lightly to maintain shape.

common_name: Paseo Rancho Verbena (Pink Cedros Island Verbena)

planting.note: Set out plants in spring after frost danger passes so roots establish before summer heat arrives.

directions: A California native shrub that produces loose, airy clusters of magenta-pink flowers almost continuously where winters are mild. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and minimal summer water once it's rooted in, since boggy soil is its main enemy. Cut it back lightly after flushes of bloom to keep the habit tidy and coax out fresh flowers, and expect visits from butterflies and bees all season.

common_name: Silver Peak Pig's Ear (Silvery Succulent Shrub)

planting.note: Set out in spring after frost danger has passed, in a spot with sharp drainage, and avoid overwatering while roots establish.

directions: Pig's Ear carries thick, powder-coated silvery leaves year-round and sends up stalks of dangling coral-apricot bells in late summer and fall that hummingbirds visit readily. Site it in full sun with sharply draining soil and let it dry out between waterings once established, since it's built for lean, dry conditions. It stays evergreen and resists deer, slugs, and snails, making it an easy anchor for a gravel or rock garden bed.

common_name: Pink Kaboom Ice Plant (South African Succulent Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun with good drainage, watering in well at first and then tapering off as roots establish.

directions: A South African ice plant that disappears under a sheet of electric pink daisy flowers each spring, with a lighter rebloom in fall, over fleshy evergreen foliage. Grow it in full sun with good drainage at planting time; once established it needs no supplemental summer water and tolerates poor or clay-heavy soil. Let it spill over a slope, wall, or raised bed edge where its mounding, spreading habit can show off.

common_name: Cameo Elegance Morning Glory (Variegated Japanese Morning Glory Vine)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, providing a trellis nearby since seedlings climb quickly.

directions: This Japanese morning glory pairs ivy-shaped leaves marbled in cream and green with magenta-crimson trumpet flowers edged in a delicate white picotee rim. Direct sow in full sun once the ground is warm and provide a trellis or obelisk for it to climb to about six feet by season's end. It flowers from summer to first frost, self-sows readily, and asks for only modest water to perform well.

common_name: Silver Carpet California Aster (Silvery Native Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil, spacing starts to knit into a groundcover within one to two seasons.

directions: A low, spreading California native that carpets the ground in shimmering silvery foliage topped with small lavender daisy flowers from summer into fall. It handles full sun to part shade and shrugs off heat, drought, clay soil, and even salt spray, making it a workhorse for difficult slopes and parking strips. Give it occasional water inland for the best appearance, and let it spread three feet or more as a weed-suppressing, deer-resistant mat.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at 70-75F; in warm climates seed can be sown directly outdoors once frost danger has passed.

directions: This tall South African annual produces pure white, bell-shaped flowers spotted with gold inside, opening in succession up spikes over many weeks. Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost since it needs a long season to bloom, then set plants out at the back of a border once nights stay warm. Foliage releases a peanut-butter scent when brushed, and the flowers draw hummingbirds and bees; watch for thrips in hot, dry weather. Water about an inch a week, more during establishment, less once the deep roots take hold.

planting.note: Surface sow and press seed in lightly 6-8 weeks before last frost since it needs light to germinate, or direct sow once frost danger passes.

directions: Native to the New Mexico mountains, this hyssop sends up hazy rose-pink flower wands above gray-green foliage and purple-flushed stems. It is slow from seed, usually building a root system in its first year and flowering heavily the next, so patience is required. Plant in sharply draining, gritty soil rather than rich moist ground, which only encourages floppy growth, and deadhead to keep blooms coming. Once established it tolerates real drought and shrugs off deer and rabbits, needing only an occasional deep soak in extended dry spells.

planting.note: Surface sow indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost; in zone 8 and warmer it can be direct sown outdoors once soil has warmed.

directions: A fast twining vine with sage-green arrowhead leaves and dangling lavender-blue trumpet flowers that draw hummingbirds and bees. Give it a trellis or thin canes to climb, or let it cascade from a hanging basket or window box. It self-cleans spent blooms so deadheading is unnecessary, but a monthly dose of compost or balanced fertilizer keeps growth vigorous. Keep soil evenly moist without letting it stay waterlogged, and expect essentially no pest or disease trouble.

planting.note: Start indoors six weeks before last frost under a humidity dome, or direct sow outdoors after frost danger passes, barely covering the tiny seed.

directions: This amaranth sends up fuzzy, multi-branched plumes blending light yellow and blush pink, giving a strawberry-and-banana effect over bushy plants. It is a heat and humidity lover that self-sows readily and shrugs off dry spells once rooted in, so avoid rich soil or heavy fertilizer that can cause weak stems and rot. Cut plumes fresh or hang them to dry for arrangements, and leave some seed heads standing late in the season since birds feed on them. It also makes an effective informal hedge or screen.

planting.note: Direct sow outdoors in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall/winter in zone 8 and warmer; this corncockle resents transplanting.

directions: A wispy old-fashioned cornfield weed turned garden flower, with open blush-pink petals that fade toward white as they age, giving a two-toned effect on wiry stems, paler than the magenta-purple of the straight species already common in wildflower mixes. Sow it where it is to grow since it dislikes root disturbance, scattering seed shallowly in early spring or, in milder climates, over fall and winter. It needs nothing more than average soil and weekly watering, attracting bees and hummingbirds while shrugging off most pests. Deadhead for a longer show, or let some pods mature for reliable self-sowing, but keep all parts away from children and pets since the seeds are toxic if eaten.

planting.note: Start indoors six weeks before last frost under a humidity dome, or direct sow outdoors after frost danger passes, barely covering the tiny seed.

directions: Unlike the typical rosy love-lies-bleeding, this strain drips with woolly, knotted burgundy-red ropes of bloom that trail dramatically to the ground. It thrives in heavy heat and humidity but should be staked in windy sites since the heavy tassels can topple stems, and it needs sharp drainage to avoid root rot. Watch young plants for flea beetle and tarnished plant bug damage, though mature plants outgrow most pest pressure. The dried flower ropes hold color well for arrangements, and birds work the ripening seed heads in fall.

planting.note: Start indoors six weeks before last frost under a humidity dome, or direct sow outdoors after frost danger passes, barely covering the tiny seed.

directions: Named for its curled, trunk-like flower spike, this stout heirloom amaranth produces deep burgundy clusters on thick stems that stand up well in heat and humidity. It needs well-drained soil to avoid root disease and does best without extra fertilizer, which pushes leafy growth at the expense of flower size. Flea beetles can chew foliage and tarnished plant bugs sometimes work into the flower heads, so check plants through the season. Cut stems once half to three-quarters of the florets have opened for the longest vase life, and let a few plants go to seed since they self-sow freely.

common_name: Carnation 'Chabaud Giants Nero' (Velvet Red Clove Carnation)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, germinating warm then cooling seedlings to 50-55F to build sturdy stems before transplanting at the frost date.

directions: This old French strain bears deep velvety red double blooms layered with ruffled petals and a strong clove fragrance that carries across a border, darker than the mixed Chabaud Giant seed strains already grown. Pinch young seedlings back to 6-8 inches to force side branching and more flowering stems, and grow it in neutral to alkaline soil with good airflow between plants to ward off leaf spot. It behaves as a short-lived perennial in warmer zones but is usually treated as an annual elsewhere, planted out once frost danger passes. The petals are edible and make an attractive, clove-scented garnish on salads or desserts.

subcategory: half-hardy annual / cool-season cut flower heirloom

planting.note: Surface sow indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, germinating warm then growing on cool at 45-50F; in cool-summer climates it can instead be sown outdoors or in a coldframe 2-3 weeks before last frost.

directions: Tapered spikes crowded with smoky cocoa-rose flowers carry a spicy clove scent reminiscent of classic old-garden stocks. This variety performs best where summers stay cool, ideally under 75F, so gardeners in hot regions should treat it as an early spring or fall crop rather than a summer bloomer. Grow it in sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil and space plants a foot apart with good airflow to prevent leaf disease. Keep moisture consistent while seedlings establish, then water about an inch weekly through bloom.

planting.note: Direct sow outdoors 3-4 weeks before last frost, barely covering seed; fall sowing in October also works in zones 7-10 for earlier bloom.

directions: This certified-organic strain carries vivid violet-purple blooms on wiry, pliant stems above silver-green foliage, a saturated departure from classic cornflower blue. Sow directly where plants will grow since cornflowers resist transplanting, and skip indoor starting entirely. It handles heat and dry spells well once established, needing only weekly water during establishment, and draws bees and other beneficial insects to the garden. Petals are edible fresh in salads or frozen into ice cubes, and stems cut just as flowers open hold up well in arrangements.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a warm, bright spot and expect several seasons of leaf growth before the first dramatic flower spikes appear.

directions: One of the darkest agapanthus selections, this clumping bulb sends up sturdy purple-black stems topped with rounded umbels of deep violet-blue to near-black trumpet flowers in mid-to-late summer. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, since waterlogging over winter is the main cause of loss. Because it is seed-raised, individual seedlings will vary somewhat in depth of color, so grow a few extra and select the darkest bloomers. Established clumps make excellent cut flowers and leave striking architectural seed heads if left standing into autumn.

planting.note: Pot on seedlings and keep them frost-free for their first couple of winters before trusting a mature clump outdoors year-round.

directions: This white-flowered agapanthus produces tight, globe-shaped heads of pure white blooms, occasionally blushed pink at the petal tips, held on stout stems above vigorous clumps of bright green strap leaves. It flowers mid-to-late summer and performs best in moisture-retentive but still free-draining soil in full sun. Clumps thicken and flower more heavily each year, so avoid dividing or disturbing an established planting unless it has become overcrowded. It makes a strong architectural counterpoint to the many blue-flowered agapanthus cultivars in a mixed border.

planting.note: This selection is noted for unusually good cold tolerance for the species, but still benefits from a dry winter mulch in marginal zones.

directions: A bicolor agapanthus whose large globular flower heads open white and carry a delicate blue brushstroke at each petal tip, set above the typical strap-shaped foliage of the genus. Originating as a chance seedling, it is reported to form heavy, long-lived clumps that improve year after year once settled into moisture-retentive soil. Give it full sun and leave the roots undisturbed, dividing only when flowering noticeably declines. Its two-tone blooms photograph beautifully against the plain blue or white agapanthus more typically seen in catalogs.

planting.note: Grow against a sheltered, sunny wall in cooler climates since this is a fast but relatively short-lived shrub that resents cold, wet winters.

directions: This soft-hued abutilon carries open, saucer-shaped flowers that shift from near-white to a chalky blue-mauve, produced in trusses against felted, greyish, vine-shaped leaves from spring well into autumn. It grows quickly into a large, loose shrub and is happiest trained against a warm wall where its brittle wood gets some shelter from wind. Keep the soil free-draining, since wet feet in winter are far more likely to kill it than cold air alone. Seedlings vary a little in flower tone, so grow a batch and keep the best-colored plants.

planting.note: Plant out after frost into a sheltered, sunny border; the fragrant flowers are edible and attract a steady stream of pollinators.

directions: A pure white-flowered form of the vine-leaf abutilon, this fast-growing deciduous shrub produces abundant, slightly fragrant blooms from April through July against downy, greyish, maple-like leaves. It is best treated as a short-lived specimen shrub, given a sheltered spot and free-draining soil to offset its sensitivity to winter wet. Because the flowers are edible, they can be used to garnish salads as well as providing weeks of ornamental display. Hard pruning after flowering keeps growth compact and encourages a bushier second season.

planting.note: Sow outdoors in autumn so winter cold naturally breaks seed dormancy, or mimic this with several months of refrigerated stratification before spring sowing.

directions: This exceptionally slow, weeping maple forms a dense, domed mound of finely cut, lace-like leaves that color through yellow, bronze, and red in autumn; a plant may take two decades to reach a single meter in height. It suits a container, rockery, or bonsai training as much as open ground, and appreciates light shade to protect the delicate foliage from scorching. Grow it in humus-rich, free-draining soil and shelter it from strong, drying winds that can shred the thin leaves. Patience is the main requirement, since this is a tree grown for decades of slow, sculptural change rather than quick impact.

planting.note: Train against a warm, sheltered wall where its evergreen foliage and odd pipe-shaped flowers can be appreciated at close range.

directions: This Mediterranean evergreen climber carries glossy, heart-shaped leaves and curious curved, pipe-shaped flowers whose pale green and reddish exterior opens to a golden, hairy throat and a dark maroon lip. The unusual bloom structure briefly traps small pollinating insects inside the flower tube before releasing them once pollination has occurred. Once its roots are established it tolerates considerable summer drought, so avoid overwatering and give it free-draining soil and a warm, sunny aspect. All parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so site it away from where children or pets might be tempted to sample it.

planting.note: Give it a trellis, fence, or shrub to scramble through, since this climbing asparagus has no tendrils of its own and relies on its wiry stems for support.

directions: An unusual climbing relative of edible asparagus, this vine scrambles up to fifteen feet on wiry, ferny stems that stay green deep into frost, with fragrant white flowers in late spring followed by bright red berries by late summer. It is remarkably cold-hardy for a climber of this type, tolerating winters far harsher than its delicate foliage would suggest. Grow it up a fence or through an open shrub in full sun with free-draining soil, and expect it to die back to the base in the coldest winters before resprouting from the roots. The berries are ornamental rather than edible, and add autumn interest once the flowers have finished.
